week.mechanism: A war fought abroad comes home as higher prices and a closed sea lane, the governing party loses a national election, and a leader inside that party names the war as the reason.

candidates.mechanism: A war fought abroad brings price and wage controls at home; on 11 March 1952 the sitting President loses his own party's New Hampshire primary to Senator Estes Kefauver, 19,800 votes to 15,927; on 29 March he says he will not run again; on 4 November 1952 his party loses the presidency.
candidates.fit_reason: A war abroad, its cost at home as price and wage controls, the sitting President beaten in his own party's first primary, his withdrawal, and his party's loss of the presidency, all inside one horizon and all on primary record.
candidates.bridge: clear on the founder's reading; the parties are named as 1952 institutions (no_bridge)

candidates.fit_reason: Sea lane, prices and a lost midterm; not checked against primary sources in this session, and no held document of a party figure naming the war.

candidates.mechanism: A war abroad, a President who tells the nation that prices and interest rates have risen because Congress has not passed his tax bill, and who on 31 March 1968 says he will not seek his party's nomination.
corrected_facts: Johnson won the 12 March 1968 New Hampshire primary as a write-in candidate; McCarthy was second (the reviewer gives about 49.6% to 41.9%; not re-read from an official count in this session). The first pick's sentence said the reverse and was false.
No national election was lost inside the 31 March 1968 horizon.
The 'prices' sentence of 31 March 1968 blames congressional inaction on the tax bill, not the war; it cannot carry the mechanism.
Guevara is not a home-front perspective.
e33-echo-02 of the first pick (the address film) is the LBJ Library's YouTube post with an unknown camera, so 'federal work' was not shown; e33-echo-08 had neither a basis nor a date.

candidates.fit_reason: Strait and cost at home; no election turns out a governing party.

mechanism_sources.price and wage controls: src-fr-19510130 (the regulation and its statement of considerations); src-truman-19510614
mechanism_sources.4 November 1952: src-stevenson-19521105 (in the horizon: the concession as printed on the morning of 5 November); src-nara-ofr-1952 is the later record only

fit_gap: Truman gave no reason tied to Korea when he withdrew; his 29 March words are used only for the withdrawal.
The New Hampshire vote is a preference poll inside one party in one state, not a national election.
Congress is not in the mechanism sentence: the 1952 House and Senate majorities were not read from a primary source in this session, and they were settled in the days after the vote.
No leader of the governing party names the war as the reason for the loss inside the horizon (the week's lead has one); none is held.

Truman's own address of 14 June 1951 says controls would be needed even if the fighting in Korea stopped tomorrow: the war is not, in his words, the only cause of the controls. The Echo reads that line (period_perspectives[0].counter).
chosen.as_of_basis: The vote was cast on Tuesday 4 November 1952; the horizon is noon in Washington the next day. The result is known inside it from Stevenson's concession as the New York Times printed it that morning (src-stevenson-19521105), so the Echo may say who won the presidency and nothing more. Official counts (the electors' votes of December 1952, the Clerk's 1953 statistics) are later records and are never shown as known at the horizon. Truman's own statement of 5 November is not used: its hour is not shown.
outside_horizon: the electors' votes of 15 December 1952 and the Clerk's printed counts
chosen.told_story: the war abroad (1951 pictures from the front); the price freeze of January 1951 on the desk; Truman's own words on prices and controls (June 1951); the New Hampshire count of 11 March 1952; the dinner of 29 March 1952 and the line he spoke there; Eisenhower's Detroit speech of 24 October 1952; the vote of 4 November.
chosen.result_rule: The result enters a spoken or printed line only through src-stevenson-19521105, which is ledgered here; no other source for it is used.

period_perspectives.who: Harry S. Truman, President (the governing party)
period_perspectives.where: broadcast from the White House, Washington
period_perspectives.quote: This is the problem of inflation and high prices.

also.quote: Now we are in a great mobilization effort. Requiring 20 percent of our national production is defense. Now our men are fighting in Korea.

period_perspectives.linked_by_speaker: In this address Truman sets price controls beside the mobilisation and the fighting in Korea himself ('Now we are in a great mobilization effort. ... Now our men are fighting in Korea.'), and in the same address says the controls would be needed even if the fighting stopped (counter).
period_perspectives.rights: public (a presidential address, a federal work)

counter.quote: Some people have the idea that if the fighting stopped in Korea we could cut down our defense effort enough to do away with the danger of inflation. That is not true. We would need controls even if the fighting in Korea stopped tomorrow. The threat of Communist aggression is worldwide, and must be met with worldwide defenses.
counter.read_from: the American Presidency Project page, sha256 5e4529bc... (the same file as src-truman-19510614), re-read on 2026-11-12; four whole sentences, contiguous
counter.note: The speaker's own counter-view: in the same address Truman says controls would be needed even if the fighting stopped. It is read by the reader right after the two lines above (rundown echo-x3), never dropped. The review's text ended at 'worldwide'; the printed sentence continues ', and must be met with worldwide defenses.', so the whole sentence is kept.
